props.title: The Face of Another
props.initialSlug: Man uses lifelike mask to seduce his own wife

sections.content: The Face of Another (1966) stands as Hiroshi Teshigahara's masterpiece of identity horror, following a businessman who receives a lifelike mask after his face is disfigured. Like Georges Franju's Eyes Without a Face (1960), it uses facial reconstruction as a gateway to explore deeper existential themes. The film's clinical aesthetic and philosophical weight drew from Japan's post-war identity crisis, while influencing later works like John Woo's Face/Off (1997) and Pedro Almodóvar's The Skin I Live In (2011).

movies.title: The Skin I Live In
movies.slug: A plastic surgeon creates synthetic skin by experimenting on a mysterious patient

sections.content: Teshigahara's experimental visual style, with its stark modernist architecture and unsettling close-ups, creates a sense of psychological fragmentation that later influenced films like Mulholland Drive (2001) and Under the Skin (2013). The film's exploration of identity through medical transformation connects to body horror classics like Videodrome (1983) and Safe (1995), where physical metamorphosis reflects psychological breakdown.

The film's themes of doubling and identity displacement echo through later Japanese cinema, particularly in works like Shinya Tsukamoto's Tetsuo: The Iron Man (1989) and Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Cure (1997). The clinical, detached tone influenced European art films like Michael Haneke's The Seventh Continent (1989) and Yorgos Lanthimos's The Lobster (2015). SUBHEAD: Identity and Modernist Architecture

sections.content: The film's use of brutalist architecture and sterile medical spaces creates a visual language of alienation that influenced later works like High-Rise (2015) and The Square (2017). Teshigahara's camera transforms Tokyo's post-war reconstruction into a maze of identity dissolution, predating similar architectural horror in films like Possession (1981) and Raw (2016).
